Keywords: systemd unit, service file, restart policy, wantedby
Guidance: A systemd service with no Restart= directive stays dead after a crash until someone notices, and missing After=/Requires= ordering can start a service before its dependency (like a database) is ready.
Do: Set Restart=on-failure (or always) with a sane RestartSec, and declare correct After=/Requires= ordering against dependencies.
Don't: Write a systemd unit with no restart policy and no explicit ordering against required dependent services.

Keywords: journalctl, systemd logs, log filtering, boot logs
Guidance: Scrolling through the entire journal with no filters to find one service's errors around a specific incident time wastes time journalctl's built-in filters solve directly.
Do: Filter journalctl by unit, priority, and time range (-u, -p, --since/--until) instead of scrolling unfiltered output.
Don't: Run journalctl with no filters and manually scroll/grep through the entire system journal.

Keywords: iptables, nftables, firewall rules, default policy
Guidance: Adding firewall rules ad hoc without a default-deny policy and without persisting rules across reboot leaves a host either overly permissive or silently unprotected after the next restart.
Do: Set a default-deny INPUT policy, explicitly allow required traffic, and persist rules (iptables-persistent or nftables config) across reboots.
Don't: Add firewall allow rules with no default-deny baseline, or forget to persist rules so they vanish on reboot.
Example: nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept

Keywords: cron, crontab, cron environment, cron failure notification
Guidance: Cron jobs run with a minimal environment (no login shell PATH, no user profile) and failures are silent by default, so a script that works interactively can fail mysteriously under cron with nobody noticing.
Do: Use absolute paths, set PATH explicitly in crontab, redirect output to a log, and alert on non-zero exit codes.
Don't: Assume a script that works when run interactively will behave identically under cron's minimal environment.

Topic: Filesystem permissions: SUID and sticky bit
Keywords: suid, sgid, sticky bit, file permissions, privilege escalation
Guidance: An unnecessary SUID binary is a direct privilege-escalation vector if it has any exploitable bug; the sticky bit on shared directories (like /tmp) prevents users from deleting each other's files.
Do: Audit for unnecessary SUID/SGID binaries regularly, and set the sticky bit on any world-writable shared directory.
Don't: Leave unnecessary SUID binaries in place, or create a world-writable directory with no sticky bit set.

Keywords: ssh hardening, password auth, root login, sshd_config
Guidance: Allowing password authentication and direct root login over SSH leaves a server exposed to credential-stuffing and brute-force attacks that key-based auth with root login disabled defeats entirely.
Do: Disable PasswordAuthentication and PermitRootLogin in sshd_config, using key-based auth and a non-root sudo user instead.
Don't: Leave PasswordAuthentication yes and PermitRootLogin yes on an internet-facing SSH server.

Topic: Disk space troubleshooting: inodes vs blocks
Keywords: inode exhaustion, disk full, df -i, no space left on device
Guidance: 'No space left on device' can happen with plenty of free disk blocks if inodes are exhausted (common with huge numbers of tiny files); df alone won't show this, you need df -i.
Do: Check both df -h (block usage) and df -i (inode usage) when diagnosing 'disk full' errors, since either can be the actual cause.
Don't: Diagnose 'no space left on device' errors using only df -h without checking inode usage via df -i.

Topic: Process and resource limits with ulimit
Keywords: ulimit, nofile, resource limits, too many open files
Guidance: A process hitting the default per-user open file descriptor limit (often 1024) under load fails with 'too many open files' even though the system has plenty of actual capacity.
Do: Set appropriate ulimit values (nofile, nproc) via systemd LimitNOFILE= or /etc/security/limits.conf for services expected to handle high concurrency.
Don't: Leave high-concurrency services on default ulimit values and discover the 'too many open files' failure only under production load.

Keywords: ss, netstat, listening ports, connection state
Guidance: Not knowing which process is actually bound to a port (or its connection state) turns a simple 'is the service listening' question into guesswork during an incident.
Do: Use ss -tlnp (or netstat as a fallback) to check listening ports and owning processes directly instead of guessing from application logs alone.
Don't: Debug 'connection refused' issues by only checking application logs without verifying the process is actually listening on the expected port.

Keywords: fstab, mount options, noatime, filesystem reliability
Guidance: Missing or incorrect fstab entries mean a manually-mounted volume won't remount automatically after reboot, silently breaking a service that expects that mount to exist.
Do: Persist mount configuration in /etc/fstab (with appropriate options like noatime for performance-sensitive volumes) rather than mounting manually per session.
Don't: Mount a required volume manually with the mount command and never add the corresponding fstab entry.

Keywords: zombie process, defunct process, process reaping, pid 1
Guidance: A parent process that never calls wait() on terminated children leaves zombie processes accumulating in the process table, which can eventually exhaust the PID limit.
Do: Ensure parent processes reap child processes (wait/waitpid), or use a proper init/supervisor (tini, systemd) as PID 1 in containers to reap orphans.
Don't: Run a container with an application as PID 1 that never reaps child processes, letting zombies accumulate.

Keywords: load average, vmstat, iowait, cpu steal time
Guidance: Reading only CPU percentage without checking iowait or steal time (relevant on virtualized/cloud hosts) misses whether a system is actually CPU-bound, I/O-bound, or starved by the hypervisor.
Do: Check load average alongside iowait and steal time (vmstat, top) to correctly diagnose whether a system is CPU-bound, I/O-bound, or hypervisor-starved.
Don't: Diagnose 'high load' purely from CPU percentage without checking iowait or steal time on a virtualized host.
